17.0.s.en: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

17.0.0.en: Christ declares, by His foreknowledge, that stumbling blocks exist in the world, that is, that a person may draw another away from God's way, whether through heresy, a bad idea, a bad example, psychological pressures, persecutions, and so on. But Christ warns of woes, that is, severe torment, for everyone who causes another to stumble, because he does not sin only against God but also leads others away and makes them fall.

17.1.0.en: This verse is also mentioned in (Mt 18:1). The little ones are any person who is weak in faith or knowledge or in any circumstance of weakness. Therefore God emphasizes the destruction of the one who causes them to stumble, expressing it by a heavy stone hung around his neck, which is the millstone with which grain is ground, and by his being cast into the sea, where he must sink and perish. That is, it would be better for him to perish before he causes another to stumble, because if he causes another to stumble, severe torment awaits him in the next life.

17.1.1.en: Examine your words, your actions and your appearance, even your laughter, lest you hurt the feelings of some and make them fall into sin.

17.2.0.en: Christ draws our attention to a clear stumbling block, which is unforgiveness, and He calls us to deal with any wrong done by someone by rebuking him. In (Mt 18:15) He instructs that the rebuke should be away from the eyes of others so as not to shame him; and if he repents, he is forgiven, but if he does not repent, he is forgiven in the heart so that he may receive God's forgiveness, as we pray in the Lord's Prayer, "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Yet the relationship between them may become very limited, or the wrongdoer may cut it off, so that there is no dealing between them at all; but the spiritual person keeps his peace, his love for him and his prayers for him.

17.3.0.en: Christ instructs us that if the wrong is repeated many times by the same person, up to seven times a day, and seven is the number of perfection, that is, however often his wrongs are repeated, there must be tolerance and forgiveness. If God rested on the seventh day, then your rest is to forgive your brother however much he wrongs you, just as God forgives you however much you sin every day.

17.4.0.en: A grain of mustard seed: a small black seed used as a spice. When it grows it becomes a tree reaching a height of three and a half meters, with large, firm roots. As a common Jewish expression, it denotes very small things...

17.4.1.en: The disciples asked Christ to increase their faith. He told them that true, living faith, even if it is small like a grain of mustard seed, is able to uproot a huge tree such as the sycamine, with roots spread out and strong in the earth, and plant it in the sea; that is, it works miracles and nothing is impossible before it.

17.4.2.en: The sycamine tree points to Satan or to sin rooted deep in the heart, and faith is able to be rid of it and of its authority and to drown it in the sea.

17.5.0.en: The natural custom to which people were accustomed, when their servants returned from their work in the field or from tending the flock, was that the servants would complete their household tasks of preparing supper for their master, and then eat themselves, not resting before finishing their work. So there is no merit for the servant in preparing his master's supper; it is his duty. Therefore none of us should boast of any good work he does, for this is a duty toward God, his Master, who bought him with His blood.

17.5.1.en: Gird yourself: tie up your loose garments so that you may be able to serve. This signifies spiritual striving throughout life.

17.5.2.en: Afterward: that is, in eternal life.

17.5.3.en: Eat and drink: the happiness and spiritual satisfaction in the Kingdom.

17.5.4.en: Spiritually, work in the field or tending the flock signifies the material works of the world in which God blesses us. But as we rise by returning to the house of our Master, which is the Church, we prepare supper for Him through service and preaching to those who are far off, and He eats and drinks the repentance and confession of those who were far away; and after this He grants us the heavenly food in eternal life.

17.6.0.en: The servant has no merit in fulfilling his duties, because he was bought with a price and ought to do his duty.

17.6.1.en: Likewise we must feel that we are God's servants; if we do all righteousness, this is our duty, and we should even consider ourselves unprofitable servants, because we fall short in our works, and God covers us and completes what we lack, and in His love even grants us the grace of sonship. Consequently, no one may claim to have extra virtues that he can give to others.

17.6.2.en: Note: Our Catholic brethren believe in a strange teaching called "the surplus merits of the saints." By this they mean that the great saints offered more virtues than God asked of them, and that it is their right as saints to give some people from this surplus credit, to make up for their deficiencies and shortcomings. This is a strange teaching which our Church rejects, because no human being has merit or surplus before God... and therefore we call this strange teaching "the heresy of the surplus merits of the saints."

17.6.3.en: If you do any righteousness or service, thank God humbly because He granted you to do this good work.

17.7.s.en: (5) The healing of the ten lepers

17.7.0.en: Christ was heading toward Jerusalem to accomplish our redemption on the Cross, and because He came for the salvation of the whole world, He passed through Galilee and Samaria, which were full of Gentiles, to preach to all and save them. He headed toward a small village in Samaria, for He seeks the needy, even those whom people do not care about, and He found ten lepers living outside the village. For although this disease was bodily, in the form of spots appearing on the skin, in the Old Testament it indicated the uncleanness of its sufferer, and if anyone was struck with it, the Law required that he live apart outside the city, tear his clothes, not cover his head with a turban, cover his mustache, and cry out to everyone who approached him, "Unclean, unclean."

17.7.1.en: All these were signs of shame so that they might lead him to repentance.

17.7.2.en: The meaning of this is that sin keeps a person away from enjoying membership in the Church and the blessings God gives His children in the Church.

17.8.0.en: These ten had heard of Jesus, His miracles and His teachings. Therefore, when they saw Him from afar, they believed in His power to heal them, and they cried out to Him, asking for His mercy to heal them.

17.9.0.en: Christ did not heal them but commanded them to go and show themselves to the priests. The Law of Moses required that a leper who was healed go to the priest to be certain of it, offer a sacrifice, and be given a certificate of his cleanness.

17.9.1.en: The faith of these ten appeared in their obedience to Christ, for they went to the priests, and because of their obedience, while on their way, they were cleansed of their leprosy.

17.9.2.en: Do you obey God's commandments, confident of their power before you see their blessing and touch it? Persevere in your spiritual striving and in carrying out God's commandments even if you find no consolations, and trust that you will finally receive blessings that cannot be expressed.

17.10.0.en: Glorified God: he believed that Jesus was from God, so he glorified God and declared his strong faith in Him by glorifying with a loud voice.

17.10.1.en: Fell down on his face: he prostrated himself before Him, in faith in His power and that He was from God.

17.10.2.en: A Samaritan: from the inhabitants of the northern kingdom. His origin was Jewish, but he had mixed with the Gentiles and had turned away from worshiping God in His temple at Jerusalem, so he was despised by the Jews. But what joined him with the nine Jews was their sharing in the disease of leprosy, which was regarded as uncleanness in everyone's eyes and a reason for their isolation outside the cities.

17.10.3.en: These ten were Jews, but one of them was a Samaritan, that is, from the group despised by the Jews because they did not hold fast to all the laws of Moses.

17.10.4.en: The nine set off, rejoicing in their healing, to meet the priests and their relatives and to return to their normal life. But this Samaritan felt that the first thing he ought to do was to thank Christ who had healed him, so he returned to Him rejoicing exultantly, prostrated himself before Him humbly, and thanked Him for His love for him.

17.11.0.en: Christ wanted to show the distinction of this Samaritan, so He asked where the nine who were cleansed were, and why they did not return to give thanks. Then He praised this Samaritan, declaring the superiority of his faith, not only in obedience but in thanksgiving and glorifying God. Thus the despised foreign Samaritan became better than the Jews who knew the Law. "Thy faith hath made thee whole" not only from the disease of leprosy but from sins and immersion in lusts, because his heart loved God, and this appeared in his thanksgiving.

17.11.1.en: Are you careful to thank everyone who helps you and does you a service, even if it is small? And do you thank God in your prayers for His daily gifts to you?

17.12.s.en: (6) The Kingdom of God within the soul

17.12.0.en: With observation: that is, with signs in the sky or human movements in a great reception of the Messiah. There are no material matters that I declare to you to watch for, because it is a spiritual kingdom over hearts. Lo here: that is, in Samaria or Galilee, the Christ appears.

17.12.1.en: Lo there: that is, in Jerusalem, where the temple of God is.

17.12.2.en: The kingdom of God is within you: that is, in your hearts, for God wants to reign over the hearts of His children. It also means within you, that is, in your midst.

17.12.3.en: The Pharisees asked Him about the time of the coming of the Kingdom, and their intent was the earthly kingdom of the Messiah. So He informed them not to be preoccupied with watching for external signs of the Kingdom, because it is a spiritual kingdom, and it is God's reign over the heart. Therefore He said, "Behold, the kingdom of God is within you," through the soul's faith and obedience to Christ, so that He reigns over it and gives it the joy of His fellowship until it reaches the heavenly Kingdom.

17.12.4.en: Take care of your personal relationship with Christ through your prayers and your readings until you feel His dwelling within you, and do not be preoccupied with His material blessings, for they are meant to lead you to love Him and to bind your heart to Him.

17.13.s.en: (7) The signs of the end of the days

17.13.0.en: Christ spoke with His disciples about the signs of the end of the world, and foretold that it would bring many afflictions and that people would long for Christ to be with them to help them face these. But sadly they will not understand the signs, since they will be immersed in lusts and the thoughts of the world. But if they repent and live by faith, the Holy Spirit will work in them as Christ worked and helped His disciples during His days on earth.

17.14.0.en: Christ declared to His children that deceivers would appear saying that Christ has come in His second coming in some place in the world, but He warned them against believing these lies, because He will appear to all mankind at one time. And He gave an illustration of His second coming, which is the appearance of lightning, which moves swiftly from one end of heaven to the other and is seen by all at one time.

17.15.0.en: Then He alerted His disciples to the necessity that Christ first suffer and be crucified by the hands of the Jews (in this generation) and die for the redemption of mankind, and rise from the dead, and only after this come in His second coming.

17.16.0.en: Christ describes the days before His second coming as being like the days before the flood of Noah, and the days of Sodom before it was burned in the time of Lot, when people were occupied with their worldly affairs, far from God and from repenting of their sins, and suddenly the flood came or fire fell upon Sodom.

17.16.1.en: So also Christ will come in His second coming suddenly, while people are distracted from Him by the lusts of the world and its passing concerns, and He will hold them to account, and none will escape except the righteous children of God.

17.17.0.en: Christ warns His believing children not to give up their spiritual elevation (he who is on the housetop) by seeking and being immersed in the lusts of the world; and whoever strives, advancing in the way of the spiritual life and the service of the Lord (working in the field), must not return to his old lusts and material attachments like Lot's wife, who perished because her heart was attached to material things and she looked back.

17.17.1.en: So whoever gives up these material things that all the world seeks saves his soul; that is, the one who seems to be wearying and destroying himself by not caring for his body's comfort and luxury is the one who saves his soul and receives blessed eternity.

17.18.0.en: Christ makes clear that His children who live in the midst of the world He will take to Himself, and He will leave the wicked to eternal torment.

17.18.1.en: The two on the bed signify the rich; those grinding at the mill signify those who work hard in their worldly life, that is, the poor and the toilers; and the two in the field signify the priests and servants working in the vineyard of the Lord.

17.18.2.en: From these three categories there will be righteous and wicked, so the one is taken to the Kingdom and the other to eternal torment.

17.19.0.en: The body signifies the crucified Christ.

17.19.1.en: The eagles are God's believing children who eat the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Church and live.

17.19.2.en: There is another view, that the body signifies Satan, who is in torment, and around him the wicked gather to be tormented forever.

17.19.3.en: From all the foregoing, we must be vigilant to repent of every sin, to guard against wicked lusts, and to care for the love of God.

17.19.4.en: The parable of the unjust judge, the Pharisee and the tax collector, the love of money, the healing of the blind man. The parable of the unjust judge (vv. 1-8):

17.19.5.en: 1- And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint; 2- saying, "There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: 3- and there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. 4- And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; 5- yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me." 6- And the Lord said, "Hear what the unjust judge saith. 7- And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? 8- I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?"

18.0.s.en: (7) The signs of the end of the days

18.0.0.en: The human being doubts whether his prayer is answered, or grows weary of it through weakness of his love for God, and he may reject persistence in prayer with a rational philosophy that God knows everything, so why the repetition? So Christ wanted to show the importance of pressing upon God in prayer, because this builds up a person's faith and shows how great his love for Him is.

18.1.0.en: A judge: responsible for ruling justly and for vindicating the wronged.

18.1.1.en: Feared not God: there is no motive in his heart to hold to justice in order to please God.

18.1.2.en: Regarded not man: he takes no account of the opinion of society, and so there is nothing that calls him to justice for the sake of public opinion.

18.1.3.en: A widow: represents the person who has no support, so she is easily wronged.

18.1.4.en: She came: her repeated resorting to the judge to ask his help with a just verdict.

18.1.5.en: Avenge me of mine adversary: she had an adversary who persisted in obstructing her from obtaining her rights.

18.1.6.en: The parable says that there was an unjust judge in one of the cities, who took no account of God or men, being proud and regarding no one. And in the same city there was a widow, that is, a weak woman without support, who asked this judge to avenge her and give her her lost right.

18.2.0.en: He would not for a while: he neglected her case and did not rule justly.

18.2.1.en: Troubleth me: her persistent pressing annoys me.

18.2.2.en: Weary me: she presses upon me with her importunity.

18.2.3.en: Because of the woman's persistence, this unjust judge was compelled to vindicate her so that she would not trouble him, and not out of sympathy for her or adherence to justice.

18.3.0.en: Hear what he saith: note what this judge said, that he would vindicate the widow because of her much importunity.

18.3.1.en: Shall not avenge: shall not return to them their rights stolen by the devil, their adversary, giving them His peace and delivering them from sin, so that they even trample the power of Satan.

18.3.2.en: His elect: God's children whom He chose out of the world because of their response to Him.

18.3.4.en: Day and night: importunity and continuing in prayer.

18.3.5.en: Though he bear long with them: God postpones the answer for a time so as to give the gift at the best time, in order to build up the faith, the love and the striving of His children; but He does not forget them, and He must vindicate them in the end and grant them His abundant gifts. If an unjust judge responds to the importunity of the wronged woman, how much more will the just and loving God respond to His children when they press upon Him in prayer, to rescue them from the wicked and from the devil's wars.

18.4.0.en: I tell you: an affirmation of what follows.

18.4.1.en: Speedily: He will not be late beyond the proper time according to His wisdom for the benefit of His children, but at the best time He grants them His gifts, especially if we look at the short span of life in comparison with eternity.

18.4.2.en: Here Christ affirms the importance of linking importunity in prayer with faith, and He asks whether at His second coming He will find strong faith in many, that is, fervent prayers with importunity.

18.4.3.en: Believe that God hears your prayers even if He delays in answering, and continue in prayer to show your love for Him and your clinging to Him.

18.5.s.en: (2) The Pharisee and the tax collector

18.5.0.en: Despised others: those who are proud fall easily into condemning and even despising others. Christ confronted a group of proud people who walked in the spiritual life with exactness but felt their own self-righteousness, so He gave them a parable through which He taught them the importance of humility.

18.6.0.en: The parable shows that all are human beings in God's sight, whatever their position, but the evaluation is according to their spiritual life and their humility. The purpose of both was prayer, and this is a holy purpose, but what matters most is how one prays.

18.6.1.en: One of them was of the Pharisees, who held fast to the Law but felt their distinction and their righteousness over others. As for the tax collector, his conduct in life was evil, bound up with love of money and harshness toward others; but the good part was that he wanted to pray and to have a relationship with God.

18.7.0.en: As other men: he puts himself in a high rank and the rest of the people in a low rank because of their evils.

18.7.1.en: The Pharisee began his prayer with thanksgiving, which is a beautiful thing, but it appeared from his thanksgiving that he felt his superiority, and even condemned people in general who had fallen into sins such as robbery, injustice and adultery; and more than this, he specifically condemned a man like himself, the tax collector who had entered to pray alongside him.

18.8.0.en: The Pharisee continued his prayer, puffed up with his self-righteousness in fulfilling the commandments such as fasting and giving tithes.

18.9.0.en: But the other person, the tax collector, felt his many sins and that he was unworthy to pray and to be in the house of God. So he stood afar off, looking at the temple with reverence and humility, and even smote his breast, declaring his remorse and repentance for all his former sins, humbly asking God's mercy and forgiveness and confessing his sins by saying, "the sinner."

18.9.1.en: The Pharisee signifies the Jewish nation, proud of its knowledge of God and His laws, while the tax collector signifies the sinful Gentiles who come humbly to Christ and so receive salvation, unlike the proud among the Jews.

18.10.0.en: I tell you: an affirmation of the importance of what follows.

18.10.3.en: The answer of heaven came in forgiveness of the humble tax collector's sins and his justification from every sin, while the proud Pharisee's prayer was rejected and even became a judgment upon him and a fixing of his sins on his head.

18.10.4.en: Then Christ our God comments on the parable, that whoever exalts himself and is proud, God rejects him and brings him down to hell, but whoever humbles himself in repentance and contrition, God honors him and exalts him to enjoy with Him the heavenly Kingdom.

18.10.5.en: Look at your sins and your weakness and you will be humbled before God, and this will move you to a strong relationship with Him in which you make up for what you have missed, and you will also look at the virtues of those around you in order to imitate them.

18.11.0.en: Some people from the crowds wanted their children to receive a blessing from Christ, so they brought them to Him that He might touch them. But the disciples felt that Christ's stature was too great for Him to care about children, so they tried to keep them away so that they would not distract their Teacher from His teachings and His healing of the sick by this trivial matter.

18.12.0.en: Christ cared for the children, and told His disciples to let the children come to Him, and He blessed them; and He even declared an important truth, namely the distinctiveness of children in their character from adults, and that those who have these traits of innocence, love for others, and appreciation of the care of those around them (as a child rejoices in the love of his parents and their gifts to him), are those qualified to enter the Kingdom of Heaven.

18.12.1.en: He did not say "of these children" but "of such," that is, those among adults who have the character of children, and not only children.

18.12.2.en: And we ought to care for the weak, for they too are in need, like children.

18.13.0.en: Also mentioned in (Mt 18:3). Christ affirmed the importance of acquiring the character of children as a condition for entering the Kingdom.

18.13.1.en: Consider the qualities of the children close to you and try to learn something from them, for God has placed them in your path not only for you to teach them but also for you to learn from them.

18.14.s.en: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

18.14.0.en: A young Jewish man came forward, as the Gospels of Matthew and Mark relate, and he was a ruler of one of the synagogues of the Jews. He asked Christ how he might inherit eternal life, and addressed Him respectfully, saying, "Good Master."

18.15.0.en: Before Christ answered his question, He asked him, "Why callest thou me good?" Are these words of reverence which some say without understanding, or do you mean that I am God, since "none is good, save one, that is, God"? Christ intends here to make the young man confront himself: does he believe in the divinity of Christ, so that he asks Him to make known to him the way to the Kingdom of Heaven; or is He in his eyes merely one of the teachers of the Jews; or is he testing Him, to see whether He will guide him according to the Law of Moses or contrary to it, so as to catch Him in an error.

18.16.0.en: Christ did not state new commandments, because He came to fulfill and not to destroy, and He directed this ruler to keep the Ten Commandments; and to confirm that He meant these commandments and not other new ones that Christ teaches, He gave him examples of them, namely "Do not commit adultery, Do not kill"...

18.17.0.en: The ruler answered quickly, declaring that he had kept the commandments from his youth. He means keeping them in the mind and literal application, and not all the depths of the commandments, as shown by the appearance afterward of his attachment to material things more than love for God, and this is contrary to the spirit of the commandments.

18.18.0.en: Christ asked him to sell his possessions and distribute the price to the poor, and to follow Christ, depending on Him alone and not on his money. Christ directed this ruler's gaze to the heavenly treasure which he would gain by works of mercy, better than earthly possessions.

18.19.0.en: Christ uncovered this ruler's sin, which was the love of money, and his heart was grieved because he could not sell his money and possessions for God's sake, and by this he judged himself unworthy of the Kingdom of Heaven. Ask yourself: are you ready, even if only in intention, to leave everything you have and keep your faith in God, or do you break the commandments while your heart is attached to material things? The practical application of leaving the love of money is a partial and gradual leaving, and giving tithes and even more than them, and doing works of mercy with everyone.

18.20.0.en: Christ declared the seriousness of the problem of attachment to money, which prevents entering the Kingdom, because the rich often depend on their money and are attached to it. "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" And the only solution is that they trust in God alone and use their money for their living needs and for doing good, and are not troubled if they lose much of it. So what is meant is not that the rich do not enter the Kingdom, but those who trust in and are attached to their money.

18.21.0.en: To show the impossibility of those who trust in their money entering the Kingdom, He gave a comparison: that a camel passing through the eye of a needle is easier than for one who trusts in his money to enter the Kingdom, that is, it is impossible for him to enter.

18.22.0.en: Those who heard felt the difficulty of giving up the love of money, but Christ encouraged all the rich by saying that nothing is impossible with God, so that with His help the rich can be rid of their attachment to money.

18.23.0.en: The disciples understood the importance of the rich leaving off the love of money, so Peter said on behalf of the disciples, "Lo, we have left all, and followed thee," though they had left nothing but worn-out nets, fishing boats and simple jobs which were their trades.

18.24.0.en: Christ answered, showing His concern for anything a person leaves for His sake, whether material possessions or emotional relationships of attachment to family, friends and loved ones, for the sake of attachment to the love of God and His service. For God compensates him manifold in this life, that is, He gives him his material needs and health and gives him favor in the eyes of all. Like the monk who leaves a limited number of relatives, so his heart opens in love for everyone and all become his loved ones; and likewise the servant who gives up some of his time and rest and the enjoyment of his relationship with those close to him for the sake of serving Christ gains many souls and all become his loved ones, and then receives what cannot be expressed, which is the happiness of eternity. Look at God's graces that you receive in peace, joy and many blessings, and you will easily give up anything for the sake of His love.

18.25.s.en: (5) Telling His disciples of His sufferings

18.25.0.en: Christ took His disciples apart to tell them of His sufferings which He would bear for the redemption of the world, these sufferings which the prophets had foretold, and He began to explain these prophecies to them, and that this would soon be fulfilled because they were heading toward Jerusalem, where all this would take place. And if Christ had spoken of leaving and detachment, He presents Himself as a practical example in leaving, even unto death, because of His love for us.

18.26.0.en: He explained to them how the Romans, that is, the Gentiles, would arrest Him, mock Him, beat Him and then kill Him, but He would rise from the dead on the third day.

18.26.1.en: If sufferings meet you, trust that blessings follow them, and the harder the sufferings, the more the blessings increase.

18.27.0.en: By this Christ wanted to prepare them to receive His sufferings, but they did not understand, because their minds were bound to the idea that Christ would be an earthly king; but after His resurrection they remembered all that He had told them and believed. Christ allowed this to be hidden from them so that they would not be alarmed and afraid, while remembering His words after the Resurrection helped them to believe.

18.28.s.en: (6) The healing of the blind man on the way to Jericho

18.28.0.en: Christ was on His way to Jerusalem, and He passed through the city of Jericho, and there He found a blind man sitting by the way begging. Christ intended to pass by at this time in order to heal him, for He does good at all times, even while walking along the road.

18.28.1.en: The blind man heard the noise of a crowd approaching him, so he asked what this was, and they told him that Jesus Christ, with the crowds, was coming toward him.

18.28.2.en: If only you would seize every opportunity to do good, even on the road or in any place you enter: pray in every place, offer encouraging words to those you meet, and help everyone who asks you.

18.29.0.en: The blind man believed that this was the awaited Messiah, the Son of David, and asked Him to have mercy on him; and because of his much crying out, the crowds in front tried to silence him so as not to trouble Christ, but he cried out and implored Christ all the more, showing a strong faith that could not be stopped.

18.29.1.en: The blind man signifies mankind, which lost its ability to see God, but if it believes in Christ and implores Him with faith and humility, it receives spiritual enlightenment and again enjoys the sight of God through the sacraments of the Church. As for the crowds in front, they signify the hindrances to faith: the lusts of the world, its preoccupations and all doubts, but God allows them to test faith, and then He pours out abundant blessings on His children.

18.30.0.en: Christ stood and asked that the blind man be brought to Him, so they brought him near to Him, and Christ asked him, "What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?", in order to affirm the importance of the human will and the spiritual striving evident in the continual crying out. The blind man said that he needed to be healed so that he might see, so Christ commanded with the authority of His divinity that he receive his sight, and his eyes were opened at once, and Christ declared the truth plainly, that the blind man's faith, which drove him in the striving of continual crying out and asking for healing, is what made Christ grant him the gift of sight.

18.31.0.en: The blind man's heart was enlightened by faith before his bodily eyes were enlightened, and when Christ gave him healing he followed Him with the crowds, thanking God, and this thanksgiving of his became a motive for all the crowds to glorify and praise Christ.

18.31.1.en: Thank God at all times for His gifts, and in times of affliction too, and you will become a light in the world, encouraging everyone to a life of thanksgiving.

18.31.2.en: Zacchaeus, the parable of the faithful servants, Christ's entry into Jerusalem. The salvation of Zacchaeus (vv. 1-10):

18.31.3.en: 1- And Jesus entered and passed through Jericho. 2- And, behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich.

18.31.4.en: 3- And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature. 4- And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way. 5- And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." 6- And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully. 7- And when they saw it, they all murmured, saying, "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." 8- And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord, "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." 9- And Jesus said unto him, "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham.

18.31.5.en: 10- For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost."
